stages.say:
“We are presenting Guardrail’s log-anomaly detection component. Our work here brings together model loading, local execution, sample selection, evaluation, and inspectable outputs. Our Guardrail pipeline uses public datasets and pretrained base models with dataset-specific checkpoints.”

Opening connection
“Can we take a group of BGL system messages and classify the group as normal or anomalous? We will follow that journey from the original logs to the final results. First we explain how the data is prepared; then we follow the saved test sample through our local inference pipeline.”

Explain this step
“The original input is a public collection of records written by the BGL system. Those records must be prepared before this model can train or evaluate on them. Preparation extracts the message fields, converts reference labels, divides records into training and test portions, and groups messages into sequences.

The training branch uses train.csv to learn adapter and projection weights. The evaluation branch uses test.csv with saved weights to generate predictions. The test labels are used afterward to check correctness, not supplied as answers during inference.

For our local demonstration, we downloaded the publicly provided test.csv and selected twenty sequences. We loaded the existing dataset-specific checkpoint. We did not regenerate the full training/test files or retrain the models during this presentation. The next sections explain both the original preparation process and the actual steps we executed.”

Point to: the two branches in the complete workflow, then the starting point in our local workflow.

Connect to the next section
“Let us begin with where these logs come from and which files we have locally.”

stages.say:
Opening connection
“Now we connect individual records to the files used by the model. The preparation code splits records into training and testing portions, then groups each portion into message windows. This explains how the files can be created. In our local run, we entered the workflow afterward by downloading the prepared test file.”

Explain this step
“We first obtain and extract the full raw archive. The script needs its directory and filename configured. Use the complete BGL raw log: start_line = 0; end_line = None. The repository currently contains hardcoded paths, so this is not a command to run unchanged.

The parser separates each record into fields and writes an intermediate structured CSV. The raw reference label is converted into zero or one. This is preparing the answer key; it is not predicting anomalies. Invalid-format records can be skipped by the existing parser.

The code then divides the parsed records in their existing order: the first eighty percent are training records and the remaining twenty percent are test records. Only after that split does it form windows separately within each portion. With a window size and step of one hundred, consecutive groups do not overlap. A final group may be shorter.

If any event in a group has reference label one, the sequence receives reference label one. The script joins each group’s messages into Content and saves the sequence label, the individual event labels, and the message count. These become train.csv and test.csv.

This preparation code exists in the repository. Our local test.csv files were downloaded already prepared, so we have not established that rerunning the current script reproduces those files exactly. Normalization and tokenization still happen afterward when the model loader reads the sequences.”

Point to: the split before windowing, the four saved columns, and the preparation command’s configuration requirement.

Connect to the next section

stages.title: Normalization before BERT
stages.explanation: We have the message text, but changing identifiers and other variable values can make similar events look different. The loader applies the existing regular-expression replacements. The before-and-after examples show this text transformation; no prediction has been made yet.
stages.say:
Opening connection
“We have the message text, but changing identifiers and other variable values can make similar events look different. The loader applies the existing regular-expression replacements. The before-and-after examples show this text transformation; no prediction has been made yet.”

Explain this step
“The dataset loader calls replace_patterns on Content. This is a deterministic regular-expression function: the same text produces the same normalized output. It masks matched patterns such as numeric identifiers, IP addresses, and file paths with the placeholder <*>. It also handles other configured patterns and reduces runs of repeated dots.

For example, two messages that differ only in a matched identifier may become identical after masking. The intention is to reduce variation from changing values so the model can process more consistent message patterns. This operation does not detect an anomaly or assign a label.

We are using the existing normalization function. It is not a newly trained template parser, and it does not guarantee an accuracy improvement. Masking can remove useful information, and its regexes can replace parts of a word or path. Later, the uncased BERT tokenizer also lowercases the text; that is a separate operation.

The before and after panels contain the same actual messages from the selected sample. We can therefore inspect exactly what this implementation removes and what remains.”

Point to: a changing value before masking and the corresponding <*> afterward. Do not describe every remaining word as an identified security feature.

stages.title: Sequence boundaries and batch construction
stages.explanation: The loader splits each sequence into individual messages. The collator collects those messages into a batch and records where sequences separate. This arrangement lets BERT process messages individually and lets the later stages reconstruct the original groups.
stages.say:
Opening connection
“The loader splits each sequence into individual messages. The collator collects those messages into a batch and records where sequences separate. This arrangement lets BERT process messages individually and lets the later stages reconstruct the original groups.”

Explain this step
“A message is one entry. A sequence is a group of entries that receives one prediction. A window is a rule for forming such groups. A batch is the number of sequences processed together in one model call.

Our prepared sample already has one hundred messages per sequence. The loader splits the Content string using the delimiter. The collator then keeps at most 128 messages per sequence and limits each tokenized message to 100 BERT tokens. These are input caps: changing them does not rebuild the original windows. With 100 messages and a cap of 128, no messages are removed from these sample sequences by that cap.

For efficiency, messages from all sequences in a batch are combined for BERT. The code records split positions so it can restore the sequence groups after encoding. With batch size one, the split-position list is empty because there is no boundary between different sequences to record.

The separate six-event example in the Terminal explains window size and stride. It is an illustration using the existing helper, not a model experiment or a change to our prepared evaluation data.”

Point to: sequence count, message count, length limits, and split positions.

stages.title: Actual BERT tokenizer output
stages.explanation: The tokenizer breaks each message into vocabulary pieces and maps those pieces to integer IDs. Padding makes the rows fit together, and the attention mask identifies padding positions. These arrays are the direct inputs to BERT.
stages.say:
Opening connection
“The tokenizer breaks each message into vocabulary pieces and maps those pieces to integer IDs. Padding makes the rows fit together, and the attention mask identifies padding positions. These arrays are the direct inputs to BERT.”

Explain this step
“The tokenizer breaks text into vocabulary pieces called tokens. A token can be a word, punctuation, or part of a word. With WordPiece tokenization, a piece beginning with ## continues a word. The placeholder <*> is also tokenized into pieces; it is not a special anomaly symbol.

Each token is mapped to an integer vocabulary ID. These IDs are lookup indices, not severity values or meaningful measurements: a larger ID does not mean a more anomalous token. BERT later looks up learned numerical embeddings for them. [CLS] marks the start and [SEP] the end of each message input. [PAD] fills shorter rows so they can be stored together.

The attention mask tells BERT which positions are real or special tokens and which are padding: one means included, zero means padding. It is not a normal/anomalous mask, nor an explanation of what BERT considers important.

In this captured BGL batch, the input shape is [100, 11]: one hundred message rows with 11 token positions per row after padding. A tensor is simply a numerical array with one or more dimensions. The width depends on this batch’s token lengths and the configured cap.”

Point to: a token, its ID at the same position, the mask, and both dimensions of the shape.

Connect to the next section

stages.say:
Opening connection
“BERT now transforms the tokenized messages into numerical representations. A vector is an ordered list of numbers; here, each message becomes 768 numbers. The dataset adapter adjusts the base model’s behavior, and the saved trace lets us inspect the resulting shape.”

Explain this step
“A vector is an ordered list of numbers. Here, a message vector contains 768 values. We also call it a numerical representation or embedding. These values are learned features, not the original token IDs and not a list of named fields such as IP address or severity. We cannot point to a single coordinate and say that it means attack or failure.

BERT first converts token IDs into embeddings and processes them through transformer layers. Its attention mechanism allows tokens within the same message to influence each other’s representations. In our implementation, each message is a separate BERT input row; BERT is not directly attending across all one hundred log messages at this step.

The code takes BERT’s pooler_output, a transformed representation of the first [CLS] position, as one fixed-length vector for each message. That gives the observed shape [100, 768]: one hundred messages, each represented by 768 numbers. The display shows only eight numbers from the first vector, not the complete tensor.

We load the dataset-specific LoRA adapter with base BERT. LoRA stores learned low-rank adjustments to selected layers. During this inference run those weights remain fixed. The vector is an intermediate representation; BERT does not output our final normal/anomalous verdict here.”

Point to: [100, 768], the eight-value excerpt, and the BERT adapter path. Positive and negative numbers are representation values, not confidence percentages.

stages.title: Projection into Llama’s representation size
stages.explanation: The projection layer takes exactly the vectors produced by BERT and applies a learned linear transformation. It keeps one row per message while changing the width from 768 to 4,096. This makes the representations compatible with Llama’s input size.
stages.say:
Opening connection
“The projection layer takes exactly the vectors produced by BERT and applies a learned linear transformation. It keeps one row per message while changing the width from 768 to 4,096. This makes the representations compatible with Llama’s input size.”

Explain this step
“BERT produces a 768-value vector per message, while this Llama model expects a 4,096-value embedding at each input position. The projection layer is a learned linear mapping that connects these two sizes. For one message, it computes y = W x + b, where x is the BERT vector, W is a learned matrix, and b is a learned bias.

The output shape is [100, 4096]. The number of message rows remains one hundred; only the representation width changes. It is not padding the BERT vector with zeros or creating 4,096 messages. The learned transformation produces a representation that the downstream model can use.

The weights are loaded from projector.pt. The captured projection values are float32 at this point; the model code then casts them to float16 before assembling Llama’s input. Float32 and float16 describe numerical precision, not prediction quality or confidence.

Like the BERT vectors, these projected values are intermediate features, not anomaly scores. Their usefulness depends on the learned weights and the rest of the model, rather than on interpreting a single displayed coordinate.”

Point to: the change from 768 to 4,096 columns, the unchanged 100 rows, the dtype, and the saved projector path.

Explain this step
“In this selected BGL run, we have 10 correctly classified normal sequences, 7 detected anomalies, 0 false alarms, and 3 missed anomalies.

Accuracy asks: out of all sequences, how many predictions were correct? It is (TP + TN) divided by the sample count. Precision asks: among sequences flagged anomalous, how many really had an anomalous reference label? It is TP / (TP + FP). Recall asks: among all reference anomalies, how many did we detect? Here the recorded accuracy is 85%, precision is 100%, recall is 70%, and F1 is 82.35%. These are aggregate scores across the selected sample, not confidence values for individual predictions. We checked their arithmetic against the saved prediction rows.

Each dataset also uses its own checkpoint, so this comparison does not show that one checkpoint generalizes to the other dataset. The BGL scores come from the earlier twenty-sequence run; its intermediate trace is a separate one-sequence observation, not a new benchmark.

We save predictions.csv for individual outputs, metrics.json for scores, and run.json for paths and execution settings. “We have the message text, but changing identifiers and other variable values can make similar events look different. The loader applies the existing regular-expression replacements. The before-and-after examples show this text transformation; no prediction has been made yet.”

Explain this step
“The dataset loader calls replace_patterns on Content. This is a deterministic regular-expression function: the same text produces the same normalized output. It masks matched patterns such as numeric identifiers, IP addresses, and file paths with the placeholder <*>. It also handles other configured patterns and reduces runs of repeated dots.

For example, two messages that differ only in a matched identifier may become identical after masking. The intention is to reduce variation from changing values so the model can process more consistent message patterns. This operation does not detect an anomaly or assign a label.

We are using the existing normalization function. It is not a newly trained template parser, and it does not guarantee an accuracy improvement. Masking can remove useful information, and its regexes can replace parts of a word or path. Later, the uncased BERT tokenizer also lowercases the text; that is a separate operation.

The before and after panels contain the same actual messages from the selected sample. We can therefore inspect exactly what this implementation removes and what remains.”

Point to: a changing value before masking and the corresponding <*> afterward. Do not describe every remaining word as an identified security feature.

stages.title: Sequence boundaries and batch construction
stages.explanation: The loader splits each sequence into individual messages. The collator collects those messages into a batch and records where sequences separate. This arrangement lets BERT process messages individually and lets the later stages reconstruct the original groups.
stages.say:
Opening connection
“The loader splits each sequence into individual messages. The collator collects those messages into a batch and records where sequences separate. This arrangement lets BERT process messages individually and lets the later stages reconstruct the original groups.”

Explain this step
“A message is one entry. A sequence is a group of entries that receives one prediction. A window is a rule for forming such groups. A batch is the number of sequences processed together in one model call.

Our prepared sample already has one hundred messages per sequence. The loader splits the Content string using the delimiter. The collator then keeps at most 128 messages per sequence and limits each tokenized message to 100 BERT tokens. These are input caps: changing them does not rebuild the original windows. With 100 messages and a cap of 128, no messages are removed from these sample sequences by that cap.

For efficiency, messages from all sequences in a batch are combined for BERT. The code records split positions so it can restore the sequence groups after encoding. With batch size one, the split-position list is empty because there is no boundary between different sequences to record.

The separate six-event example in the Terminal explains window size and stride. It is an illustration using the existing helper, not a model experiment or a change to our prepared evaluation data.”

Point to: sequence count, message count, length limits, and split positions.

stages.title: Actual BERT tokenizer output
stages.explanation: The tokenizer breaks each message into vocabulary pieces and maps those pieces to integer IDs. Padding makes the rows fit together, and the attention mask identifies padding positions. These arrays are the direct inputs to BERT.
stages.say:
Opening connection
“The tokenizer breaks each message into vocabulary pieces and maps those pieces to integer IDs. Padding makes the rows fit together, and the attention mask identifies padding positions. These arrays are the direct inputs to BERT.”

Explain this step
“The tokenizer breaks text into vocabulary pieces called tokens. A token can be a word, punctuation, or part of a word. With WordPiece tokenization, a piece beginning with ## continues a word. The placeholder <*> is also tokenized into pieces; it is not a special anomaly symbol.

Each token is mapped to an integer vocabulary ID. These IDs are lookup indices, not severity values or meaningful measurements: a larger ID does not mean a more anomalous token. BERT later looks up learned numerical embeddings for them. [CLS] marks the start and [SEP] the end of each message input. [PAD] fills shorter rows so they can be stored together.

The attention mask tells BERT which positions are real or special tokens and which are padding: one means included, zero means padding. It is not a normal/anomalous mask, nor an explanation of what BERT considers important.

In this captured Liberty batch, the input shape is [100, 71]: one hundred message rows with 71 token positions per row after padding. A tensor is simply a numerical array with one or more dimensions. The width depends on this batch’s token lengths and the configured cap.”

Point to: a token, its ID at the same position, the mask, and both dimensions of the shape.

Connect to the next section
“These IDs identify vocabulary entries. BERT processes them to produce a learned representation of each message.”

stages.title: BERT output with the dataset adapter
stages.explanation: BERT now transforms the tokenized messages into numerical representations. A vector is an ordered list of numbers; here, each message becomes 768 numbers. The dataset adapter adjusts the base model’s behavior, and the saved trace lets us inspect the resulting shape.
stages.say:
Opening connection
“BERT now transforms the tokenized messages into numerical representations. A vector is an ordered list of numbers; here, each message becomes 768 numbers. The dataset adapter adjusts the base model’s behavior, and the saved trace lets us inspect the resulting shape.”

Explain this step
“A vector is an ordered list of numbers. Here, a message vector contains 768 values. We also call it a numerical representation or embedding. These values are learned features, not the original token IDs and not a list of named fields such as IP address or severity. We cannot point to a single coordinate and say that it means attack or failure.

BERT first converts token IDs into embeddings and processes them through transformer layers. Its attention mechanism allows tokens within the same message to influence each other’s representations. In our implementation, each message is a separate BERT input row; BERT is not directly attending across all one hundred log messages at this step.

The code takes BERT’s pooler_output, a transformed representation of the first [CLS] position, as one fixed-length vector for each message. That gives the observed shape [100, 768]: one hundred messages, each represented by 768 numbers. The display shows only eight numbers from the first vector, not the complete tensor.

We load the dataset-specific LoRA adapter with base BERT. LoRA stores learned low-rank adjustments to selected layers. During this inference run those weights remain fixed. The vector is an intermediate representation; BERT does not output our final normal/anomalous verdict here.”

Point to: [100, 768], the eight-value excerpt, and the BERT adapter path. Positive and negative numbers are representation values, not confidence percentages.

Connect to the next section
“We now have message vectors, but Llama expects 4,096 values per input position. The projection layer bridges that size difference.”

stages.title: Projection into Llama’s representation size
stages.explanation: The projection layer takes exactly the vectors produced by BERT and applies a learned linear transformation. It keeps one row per message while changing the width from 768 to 4,096. This makes the representations compatible with Llama’s input size.
stages.say:
Opening connection
“The projection layer takes exactly the vectors produced by BERT and applies a learned linear transformation. It keeps one row per message while changing the width from 768 to 4,096. This makes the representations compatible with Llama’s input size.”

Explain this step
“BERT produces a 768-value vector per message, while this Llama model expects a 4,096-value embedding at each input position. The projection layer is a learned linear mapping that connects these two sizes. For one message, it computes y = W x + b, where x is the BERT vector, W is a learned matrix, and b is a learned bias.

The output shape is [100, 4096]. The number of message rows remains one hundred; only the representation width changes. It is not padding the BERT vector with zeros or creating 4,096 messages. The learned transformation produces a representation that the downstream model can use.

The weights are loaded from projector.pt. The captured projection values are float32 at this point; the model code then casts them to float16 before assembling Llama’s input. Float32 and float16 describe numerical precision, not prediction quality or confidence.

Like the BERT vectors, these projected values are intermediate features, not anomaly scores. Their usefulness depends on the learned weights and the rest of the model, rather than on interpreting a single displayed coordinate.”

Point to: the change from 768 to 4,096 columns, the unchanged 100 rows, the dtype, and the saved projector path.

Connect to the next section
“The vectors are now the right size. We can combine them with the task instructions and ask Llama to classify the sequence.”

stages.explanation: The model restores the sequence groups and places their projected vectors alongside the instruction and question embeddings. Llama uses this combined input and its dataset-specific adapter to generate a short classification response. This is where the model produces its answer.
stages.say:
Opening connection
“The model restores the sequence groups and places their projected vectors alongside the instruction and question embeddings. Llama uses this combined input and its dataset-specific adapter to generate a short classification response. This is where the model produces its answer.”

Explain this step
“The input is a sequence of embeddings, not a CSV file or a plain-text copy of every original log. The code combines embeddings of the instruction, one projected vector per message, embeddings of the question, and the answer prefix ‘The sequence is’. This gives Llama the task instruction together with the encoded log sequence.

The observed shape [1, 124, 4096] means one sequence in the batch, 124 input positions, and 4,096 values at every position. In this example, one hundred positions represent log messages and the remaining 24 come from the surrounding prompt. The shape can change for a different sequence length.

Llama uses its base weights and the dataset-specific adapter. It predicts scores called logits for possible next tokens. Our code selects the highest-scoring token using argmax and continues generating, reusing cached attention information. It stops when the sequence finishes or reaches the code’s short answer-length cap.

The generated token IDs are decoded into text such as ‘normal.’ or ‘anomalous.’. The reference label is not part of this prompt. We do not report the logits as calibrated confidence, and this short classification response does not explain which individual message caused the decision.”

Point to: the input’s three dimensions, the prompt composition, generated IDs, and decoded text.

stages.explanation: The evaluator converts the response into a class and compares it with the reference label withheld from inference. stages.say:
Opening connection
“The evaluator converts the response into a class and compares it with the reference label withheld from inference. This connects each original sample row to its prediction and outcome. An anomalous prediction is a correct detection only when its reference label is also anomalous.”

Explain this step
“The evaluator reads the generated text and maps normal to zero and anomalous to one. An answer that cannot be parsed as either class raises an error rather than being silently treated as normal.

Prediction is the model’s answer. Reference label is the dataset’s answer. A reference of one and prediction of one is a detected anomaly, or true positive. Zero and zero is a correctly classified normal sequence, or true negative. Reference zero with prediction one is a false alarm. Reference one with prediction zero is a missed anomaly.

Sample index identifies the row in our selected input. Source row links that row back to the publicly provided test CSV. This lets us inspect the input associated with a prediction. It does not establish a causal explanation of the model’s decision.

These records are from a completed real inference run. Opening this presentation or running the results walkthrough reads those saved records; it does not secretly start another model run. Each verdict applies to an entire sequence, so it should not be presented as a precise attack category or a highlighted offending log line.”

stages.explanation: We have now followed the complete local path: a prepared Liberty sequence became normalized text, token IDs, BERT vectors, projected vectors, and a Llama response. stages.say:
Opening connection
“We have now followed the complete local path: a prepared Liberty sequence became normalized text, token IDs, BERT vectors, projected vectors, and a Llama response. Comparing responses with reference labels gives the counts and scores below. These results describe our selected twenty-sequence run.”

Explain this step
“In this selected Liberty run, we have 10 correctly classified normal sequences, 10 detected anomalies, 0 false alarms, and 0 missed anomalies.

Accuracy asks: out of all sequences, how many predictions were correct? It is (TP + TN) divided by the sample count. Precision asks: among sequences flagged anomalous, how many really had an anomalous reference label? It is TP / (TP + FP). Recall asks: among all reference anomalies, how many did we detect? It is TP / (TP + FN). F1 is the harmonic mean of precision and recall, 2PR / (P + R).

Here the recorded accuracy is 100%, precision is 100%, recall is 100%, and F1 is 100.00%. These are aggregate scores across the selected sample, not confidence values for individual predictions. We checked their arithmetic against the saved prediction rows.

Both samples deliberately contain ten normal and ten anomalous sequences. They do not reflect the full datasets’ class distributions. Each dataset also uses its own checkpoint, so this comparison does not show that one checkpoint generalizes to the other dataset. The BGL scores come from the earlier twenty-sequence run; its intermediate trace is a separate one-sequence observation, not a new benchmark.

We save predictions.csv for individual outputs, metrics.json for scores, and run.json for paths and execution settings. These records support inspection and rerunning with the same settings, but they do not guarantee bit-for-bit results on every environment or prove who originally trained the weights.”

Point to: confusion counts first, then scores and run settings.
